Why I Won’t Bid on Every SAP S/4HANA Transformation Under RISE with SAP

By Brian W. Mead | Touchstone AI Technology Consulting Partners

Winning the contract is not the same as winning the business. 

Not all SAP Professional Services work is good business. In many cases, it’s a failure before it starts. 

For those Companies that are preparing a S/4 Rollout hiring their own Project Team, Run and Run Fast. 

If the mindset is that of the old R/3 or ECC upgrade and rollout stay away. 

After three decades in the SAP ecosystem, I have learned that some implementation opportunities are better left alone.

When a consultancy accepts an entire transformation at a price that cannot reasonably support the work, it puts its people, profitability, reputation—and the client’s outcome—at risk.

Some firms may accept an initial loss to secure a strategic account. That is their decision. But if the economics depend on future change orders, optimistic staffing assumptions, or an unrealistically smooth implementation, the engagement begins on fragile ground.

I am interested in accountable work with defined boundaries.

At Touchstone AI Technology Consulting Partners, our approach is to own specific portions of the implementation where our expertise can make a measurable difference:

* Business process discovery and translation into SAP requirements.
* Integration architecture and clearly scoped interface delivery.
* Data readiness, migration, and validation workstreams.
* Platform governance and technical modernization.
* Defined testing, stabilization, and post-go-live support.

Each engagement needs a clear statement of work, named responsibilities, documented dependencies, measurable deliverables, acceptance criteria, and disciplined change control.

A bounded workstream still carries responsibility. It must fit the overall program, and someone must own the coordination across teams.

I would rather own a clearly defined commitment and deliver it exceptionally well than accept an entire program on economics I cannot defend.

That protects the client. It protects our consultants. And it protects our ability to stand behind our work.

Touchstone AI Technology Consulting Partners.
Specific expertise. Defined deliverables. Accountability we can stand behind.

352 days. No Job. Countless applications. No interviews. The only reply I get: “Unfortunately, we will not be moving forward.”

In 13 days, it will be a full year without a job. Since returning home in February, after my bank extended my visa sponsorship for three months, this has been a very tough phase.

Some context. I left a stable job to pursue my master’s in the UAE. After a discount, tuition plus accommodation and living costs came to roughly 100,000 dirhams. Work visa options were limited and the market was not kind. I am not blaming any country or its people. It was my decision, and I should have weighed my other options more carefully.

Since February, I have applied to roles on LinkedIn in India, abroad, anywhere I could. I rewrote my CV and cover letter for each job description, matched keywords and followed ATS formatting. The only replies I received were automated emails saying “unfortunately, we will not be moving forward.” No interview. Not even a screening call.

So I tried referrals. I sent cold messages and waited three to four months between follow-ups so I would not bother anyone. Many people read my messages. Very few replied, and most who did said “best of luck.” Former colleagues told me hiring is frozen, and that any opening goes to internal contract staff first.

I understand everyone is busy, and I am not angry at anyone. But I am left asking: if applications go to automated filters and referrals go to silence, how is a job seeker supposed to be seen? And what is LinkedIn for, if connecting rarely leads to a conversation?

To anyone considering further study: ask for real placement outcomes before you pay, and ask which current skills, like AI, the course will actually teach. A degree can open a door, but it does not guarantee anyone will invite you in.

I am Gen Z too, and some days there are no words for this feeling. I am grateful for my family’s support, and I know many people do not have that. I am still holding on, with hope. If you are in the same place, you are not alone.

If you are hiring, or know someone who is, even a one-line reply would mean a great deal to me.

I went back to engineering. I didn’t write the code.

Twenty-five years ago I started as a software engineer. The path since then went through testing, production support, service delivery leadership, and eventually portfolio, performance and business management. Further from a keyboard with every step.

A few weeks ago I went back to it. Not by writing code by hand, but by directing an AI engineering agent the way I would direct a team: setting the requirements, demanding a missing test scenario, and reviewing the architecture and documentation before calling anything done.

The agent builds what you specify. The test I had to ask for turned up two real defects. The quality of the build was the quality of my requirements and my tests, which is the work leaders already know how to do.

The other thing is a choice I made on purpose. Every leadership team I have worked with asks some version of the same question each month: why doesn’t actual match forecast, and what actually caused it? So I built a working prototype that reconciles actuals against forecast and traces every flagged variance to the person, contract or server behind it — not just "here's the gap," but "here's why". It is a prototype, not a production system, and it runs on synthetic data. 
There is no AI in the prototype itself, only plain, deterministic rules. When every number has to be defensible to a finance leader, logic you can trace beats a model you can’t fully explain. The AI was in how I built it, not in what it does.

This isn’t my first time. For one business unit I delivered the MVP that digitised workforce insight, forecasting and hiring requests. A central team later took the concept enterprise-wide, with more features and a different design, given the scale. The pattern is the same each time: manual work everyone accepts as normal, until someone makes it traceable.
The real shift is not that AI can write code. It’s that a domain expert can now take a working prototype from idea to demo directly, and bring engineering in for what it takes to scale, secure and run it.

For those of us who lead delivery organisations: what does that do to how we staff and structure this work?

Every time the law changed, HR policies and procedures had to be amended after the fact. I spent years doing that across seven APAC jurisdictions: reviewing existing practice, closing the gaps, and making sure every decision could be defended if a regulator, an employee or a tribunal asked "why?"

AI in HR is that moment again. Most organisations already use it in CV screening, interview scoring and performance analytics, often under policies written before these tools existed. And regulators are landing in the same place: the employer stays accountable, not the algorithm.

The policy gap is real. SHRM's 2026 research found fewer than half of organisations have formal AI governance policies, and Adecco Group data shows 34% of companies have no policy guiding AI use at all.

🇸🇬 MAS finalised its AI Risk Management Guidelines on 7 October 2026. They cover all AI a financial institution uses, including tools bought from vendors, with expectations phasing in from October 2027. That includes the AI in your HR systems.

🇸🇬 Under Singapore's upcoming Workplace Fairness Act, MOM has been clear that AI tools must meet the same fair, merit-based standards. TAFEP's guidance: use job-related data only, and keep final decisions with people.

🇪🇺 The EU has pushed its high-risk AI rules to December 2027, but AI used in hiring, promotion and performance management remains high-risk.

Making existing practice defensible means:
▪ An inventory of every AI tool already touching an employment decision
▪ Policies and procedures amended to say where AI can and can't be used
▪ Vendor contracts that require independent assurance, not self-attestation
▪ Documented, job-related criteria for each tool
▪ Human review before any hire, promotion or exit, with a record of it
▪ Training so HR teams can spot automation bias

If a decision can't be explained, it can't be defended. The time to fix that is before the first challenge, not after.

How far along is your organisation?

On Friday I attended UXCamp Naarm | Melbourne and Maxy Lotherington's refreshing keynote kicked it off by reigniting why I got into design over a decade ago: throw out the fake rules, creating our own lenses, staying creative and saying it all with bold colours, a bubbly font and hand-drawn illustrations. It made design feel fun again.
 
With AI-designed flyers crowding my feeds, fear-mongering about our jobs, and redundancies, Maxy's keynote and the conference overall was a much-needed breath of fresh air.

I chose to attend talks that weren’t all about AI. Our industry predates it, and I wanted to hear what else designers and teams are grappling with. Highlights:
 
Rebecca Devasagayam on social contracts, the informal agreements that help us navigate misunderstandings and frustrations
Luke McManus on feedback architecture and the value of closing feedback loops
Olga Murzenkova on neuroscience and taking care of our personal state with joy and drive
Florencia Mostaccio on using accessibility better 
Tiffany C. on first-principles thinking in e-commerce, breaking down tiny moments in a user’s journey 
Janie Asencio on vibe coding, which gave her trauma but definitely gave me inspiration watching how their team uses it
Viv Dinh closing with her very articulate hiring manager advice in the locknote
 
This was my second UXCamp, and the format is human-centred design in a nutshell. Anyone can pitch, we vote for our top 5, and the schedule builds live, with the most-voted talk taking the locknote. A conference designed by its audience, where we felt heard, seen and like we mattered. Simple input, simple output, no overengineering, and definitiely no back-and-forth of prompts.

I’d forgotten how isolating it gets working solo between gigs as a contractor and freelancer. Spending a day with designers at every stage, from wide-eyed newcomers to those of us a little burnt out and cynical, really helped me reconnect with this passionate community. I loved getting to know all of you and hear what you've been up to Farhana Ismail, Salaj Arjun, Laura Chauca, Tanuj Aggarwal, Farida Shebubakar, Emily Enrica.
 
Thank you to the UXCamp Naarm | Melbourne team for curating it with so much love, the welcoming volunteers, and the very enthusiastic MC duo dressed as camp cadets  ✨

Some highlights:  

1/ When his first company ran out of runway, he left college, cold called 100 manufacturers a day, and offered to sit in their offices for free.  

2/ Pactle (backed by South Park Commons), came from spending 45 days in one of the offices. And identifying a huge leak in the sales process.  

3/ Fundraising can be made deterministic. Instead of "waiting" for it to fall in place. How? Watch.  

4/ When you're raising, your story has to answer what investors doubt about you. As a solo founder from BIT Mesra, Rohit's answer was $20,000 in signed contracts.  

5/ On hiring - after some "mistakes", he hires for the story. Ask people what they've done, and look for a lot done in a short time.  

6/ His test for dangerous delusion: if the best people in your field don't rate your work, stop.

AI interviews, Tencent's restructuring, and a court ruling on "silent terminations" — here's what HR leaders need to know today. 👇

• **AI interview bias is real** — As AI screening tools go mainstream in campus hiring, algorithm errors in facial/voice analysis are raising fairness red flags. Best practice: pair AI screening with mandatory human review before final decisions.

Contract hiring isn't a stopgap any more. It's becoming part of how companies plan their teams.

A new Express Employment Professionals / Harris Poll survey (11 Nov) of 1,006 US hiring decision-makers found:

71% of companies now build contract workers into their staffing strategy
80% of hiring managers say they're likely to hire contractors in future
25% planned to hire temp or contract workers this autumn, up from 16% in spring 2025

Separately, Principal's Financial Well-Being Index (reported by Staffing Industry Analysts, 13 Nov) found 72% of business leaders have hired flexible or specialised talent, and 58% are turning to AI and automation to manage cost pressure.

Source: https://lnkd.in/eJsrE7B9
Candidates are open to it too. In the same Express survey, 57% of job seekers have worked as contractors, and flexible hours (59%) is the top draw.
But contract hiring often goes wrong because it gets treated as second-class hiring. Here's how to get it right.

For companies:
→ Write a real brief: outcomes, timeline and who signs off. "Help with the backlog" isn't a brief.
→ Onboard contractors properly. Day-one access and context decide whether they're productive in week one or week four.
→ Be honest about whether a permanent role is possible. Don't dangle one you won't offer.
For recruiters:
→ Screen for delivery, not just skills. Ask what they shipped in their last three contracts and how long it took them to ramp up.
→ Agree on rates, notice and extension terms at the start, not at the end of the contract.

For candidates:
→ Treat each contract like a case study. Record the problem, what you did and the result.
→ Put the cost of gaps between contracts into your rate.
→ Ask what success looks like at 30 days. It tells you how organised the client is.

Done well, contract hiring is good for both sides: flexibility for the person and speed for the business.

Congratulations! You're hired, no interview needed, and we’ll pay you $180 per file just to run an AI tool! 🚨

Sounds like a dream remote accounting gig, right? It’s a trap.
Earlier this week, I applied for a remote "AI Accounting & Finance Reviewer" role after receiving a referral code. Less than 48 hours later, with zero interviews and zero technical assessments, an "official" acceptance letter landed in my inbox.
They used the stolen branding and New Zealand office address of a real global company (CHG-MERIDIAN), complete with glossy PDFs, a fake $685 starter invoice, and login credentials for a sketchy third-party "AI Excel" portal.
The catch? To "withdraw" my supposed earnings, I had to send over: 

❌ A clear copy of my Government ID / Driver’s License 
❌ My educational certificates 
❌ My bank account / IBAN / SWIFT details


Let’s call this out for what it is: a classic Task & Identity Theft Scam.
Scammers are aggressively targeting accountants, finance professionals, and remote job seekers using stolen corporate identities and buzzwords like "AI Auditing." Once they have your ID and certificates, they steal your identity, or trap you into paying fake "tax/withdrawal fees" on a rigged dashboard.


How to spot this scam before it’s too late: 

🚩 Instant hiring with no interview: Legitimate companies don't hand out $5,000–$12,000/month contracts over a single email. 
🚩 Unrealistic pay for basic tasks: Offering $100–$180 per file just to upload spreadsheets to an "AI bot" makes zero business sense. 
🚩 Lookalike domains: Always verify the sender's domain against the real company's official website. 
🚩 Upfront ID & banking grabs: Never email your national ID, degrees, or bank details to unverified recruiters.


Stay sharp out there. If an opportunity skips every normal hiring step and rushes you toward a payout form, walk away.
Share this to protect fellow finance professionals and job seekers in your network! 👇
